articles.title: China October exports beat forecasts, imports surge 41.6% as trade surplus narrows
articles.description: Stronger-than-expected exports suggest physical demand for AI hardware held up through October, offering some support to Asian tech and supply-chain stocks after last week’s selloff. The import surprise is the more notable signal. If it reflects firmer domestic demand rather than just higher commodity prices, it would be a positive for commodity exporters and the Australian dollar, which also trades as a China proxy. If higher oil prices drove much of the gain, it points to the energy shock lifting China’s import bill. A narrower surplus may slightly ease trade frictions ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, though the year-to-date surplus remains very large. - Earlier: FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy China’s trade engine is running hot in both directions, with AI hardware still flying out and a surprise surge in imports eating into the surplus. Summary: China’s October exports rose 35.2% year on year in dollar terms, beating the 33.5% forecast but slightly slower than September’s 36.3% Imports jumped 41.6%, far above the 32% expected and up from 31% in September The trade surplus narrowed to about $105 billion, short of the roughly $126 billion forecast and down from about $134 billion AI-related hardware has been the main driver of China’s export boom this year Import drivers are unclear pending the detailed data; higher commodity prices may be a factor China’s exports grew faster than expected in October and imports surged well beyond forecasts, sharply narrowing the monthly trade surplus as trade flows stayed exceptionally strong. Exports rose 35.2% from a year earlier in US dollar terms, ahead of the 33.5% median forecast in a Reuters poll, though slightly slower than September’s 36.3% gain. Imports jumped 41.6%, far above expectations for a 32% rise and accelerating from 31% the previous month. The stronger import bill cut the trade surplus to about $105 billion, well short of the roughly $126 billion forecast and down from about $134 billion in September. The export figures add to evidence that the global race to build AI infrastructure is still driving demand for Chinese-made hardware. Economists say shipments of components such as printed circuit boards, memory chips and optical transceivers have powered the surge in outbound trade this year. The October data suggest that momentum held up even as US AI stocks sold off on concerns over the pace of the data centre build-out. Some analysts had warned that a drop in new export orders in factory surveys could signal a softer tech cycle, but there is little sign of that in the headline numbers so far. The import surge is harder to read without a detailed breakdown. Higher prices for crude oil and other commodities would lift the value of China’s purchases, and inbound shipments of chips and other components for assembly would also add to the total. The full customs data, due later, should show how much of the rise reflects prices rather than volumes. The figures arrive at a sensitive moment for Beijing. Chinese stocks have been under heavy pressure, prompting authorities to step up support measures, and trade is expected to feature when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later this month. China’s large and persistent trade surplus has also risked antagonising trading partners, and a narrower monthly gap may ease some of that pressure at the margin. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
